extracted.intended_audience: immigration applicants, sponsors, practitioners, and adjudicators (stakeholders in public charge determinations)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural guidance for determining whether a noncitizen is "likely at any time to become a public charge" under INA §212(a)(4), including what evidence may be considered for factors such as assets, income, education, skills, and Affidavit of Support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Totality of the circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: A public charge inadmissibility determination is based on the totality of the noncitizen's circumstances; no one factor, other than the lack of a sufficient Affidavit of Support Under Section 213A of the INA, if required, is the sole criterion for determining if a noncitizen is likely at any time to become a public charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS will consider multiple factors (age, health, family status, assets/resources/financial status, education and skills, and current or past receipt of public benefits) together rather than prioritizing any single element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory minimum factors to consider
rubrics_metrics.description: Officers are required under section 212(a)(4) of the INA to consider specific minimum factors: the noncitizen's age; health; family status; assets, resources, and financial status; and education and skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS cannot limit the determination to only one factor and must consider all statutory minimum factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assets, resources, and financial status — permissive evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS has not established any required evidence a noncitizen must submit to establish the income, assets, and liabilities of the noncitizen's household, and as such, will consider any evidence a noncitizen chooses to submit regarding this factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If more information is needed, DHS may request additional evidence prior to making a decision; DHS did not specify particular initial evidence that must be submitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Household income, assets, and liabilities (household approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will consider a noncitizen's household's income, assets, and liabilities when considering the assets, resources, and financial status factor of a public charge inadmissibility determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS believes considering the entire household creates a more accurate representation of finances and will therefore consider income/assets/liabilities of household members (excluding income from public benefits listed in 8 CFR 212.21(b) and income or assets from illegal activities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Income from illegal activities excluded
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will not consider income or assets from illegal activities or sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Income derived from illegal activities or sources should be excluded from consideration including, but not limited to, income gained illegally from drug sales, gambling, prostitution, or alien smuggling because of policy interests and because it would be unwarranted to assume continued receipt of such income.

rubrics_metrics.name: Income from unauthorized employment may be considered
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will consider any income derived from employment in the public charge inadmissibility determination in the totality of the circumstances, regardless of whether the household members had employment authorization, as long as the income is not derived from illegal sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether the applicant engaged in unauthorized employment and any immigration consequences flowing from such employment is a separate determination from the public charge inadmissibility determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public benefits income not treated as income for assets factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Income from public benefits should not be considered as income for the purposes of a public charge inadmissibility determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS nonetheless will consider specific benefits received as evidence of 'primarily dependent' (see definition of public cash assistance for income maintenance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'primarily dependent' / evidence of public charge
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS defines 'likely at any time to become a public charge' as likely at any time to become primarily dependent on the government for subsistence, as demonstrated by either the receipt of public cash assistance for income maintenance or long-term institutionalization at government expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By focusing on cash assistance for income maintenance and long-term institutionalization, DHS aims to identify individuals primarily dependent on government subsistence without interfering with other benefit programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'public cash assistance for income maintenance'
rubrics_metrics.description: Public cash assistance for income maintenance is defined as SSI, TANF, State, Tribal, territorial, or local cash benefit programs for income maintenance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These programs constitute the best evidence of primary government dependence according to DHS consultation with benefits-granting agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of specific benefits received
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will consider the specific benefits a noncitizen receives rather than treating public-benefit-derived income neutrally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific benefit receipt (e.g., receipt of cash assistance) can be probative of primary dependence even though benefit-derived payments are not counted as income for the assets factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: No fixed minimum income threshold or presumptions based solely on income
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS declines to establish a minimum income requirement or a presumption of admissibility based on household income (e.g., 125% or 300% of the Federal Poverty Guidelines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Income is not the sole criterion; establishing a presumption based on a single income threshold would be inconsistent with the totality of circumstances approach and statutory requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of non-tax-form income and expected future income
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will not limit consideration of income to only income that appears on United States Federal income tax forms, and will consider all evidence submitted of income from lawful sources such as child support, alimony, Social Security income, investment income, and any evidence pertaining to expected future income.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS will consider such evidence if submitted, but will not independently assess expected income (e.g., will not independently evaluate labor certifications unless provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of job offers or labor certification
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will not independently assess expected income based on a labor certification and associated prevailing wage, but may consider this evidence or evidence of a job offer and estimated salary if submitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such evidence may be weighed as part of the totality of circumstances when presented by the applicant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit of Support — favorable but not dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will favorably consider a sufficient Affidavit of Support Under Section 213A of the INA, along with the statutory minimum factors, in the totality of the circumstances when assessing an applicant's likelihood at any time to become a public charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS disagrees that a sufficient Affidavit of Support alone should be deemed sufficient to overcome a public charge inadmissibility determination or that it should create a rebuttable presumption of admissibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit of Support — nature and timing of obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Affidavit of Support Under Section 213A of the INA is a contract where the sponsor agrees to provide support at an annual income not less than 125% of the FPG and to be jointly and severally liable for reimbursement obligations; these sponsorship obligations do not go into effect until after the intending immigrant's application for admission or adjustment of status is granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The contractual nature and timing of sponsor obligations are reasons DHS treats a submitted Affidavit of Support as favorable evidence but not automatically dispositive.

rubrics_metrics.name: I-134 Declaration of Financial Support not acceptable substitute
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will not accept Form I-134, Declaration of Financial Support, as a substitute for a required Affidavit of Support Under Section 213A of the INA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The I-134 is intended to demonstrate support during a temporary stay and is therefore not a valid substitution for the statutory Affidavit of Support in this context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education and skills — inclusion and broad definition
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will consider the noncitizen's education and skills as one statutory factor and defines education and skills broadly to include degrees, certifications, licenses, skills obtained through work experience (including volunteer and unpaid opportunities) or educational programs, and educational certificates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This broad interpretation is intended to encompass diverse backgrounds and occupations, including those not requiring official licenses or formal degrees.

rubrics_metrics.name: English proficiency assessed in context
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will consider English language skills in the context of the totality of circumstances; inability to speak English alone is not determinative of employability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS declines to exclude or require English proficiency as a standalone criterion; it may be considered alongside other factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unpaid or volunteer experience may demonstrate skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Skills obtained through volunteer and unpaid opportunities may be considered under the education and skills factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS acknowledges unpaid labor can equip a noncitizen with occupational skills relevant to employability.

rubrics_metrics.name: No prescriptive 'high demand' skill standard or earnings threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS declines to require demonstration of 'high demand' skills or a specific earnings standard (e.g., ability to earn three times the FPG) to establish that a noncitizen is unlikely to become a public charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS found such standards would impose an increased evidentiary and adjudicative burden and lack adequate supporting evidence correlating education/skills to public charge risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: No special carve-outs or different standards for specific groups
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS disagrees that different standards of the statutory minimum factors should be applied to different groups (e.g., children, primary caregivers, certain retirees) and will not apply distinct criteria solely because of group membership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS acknowledges concerns about disparate impact but states determinations must be based on the individual's totality of circumstances rather than categorical exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of prior records and previously submitted evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will review the noncitizen's record, including previous applications and petitions and the associated evidence, while making a public charge inadmissibility determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants who previously submitted evidence of education, skills, or employment may have that evidence considered; DHS is updating information collection to allow applicants to indicate specifics regarding education and skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjudicative burden and administrability considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will not create or require a separate information collection or form to establish admissibility and will decline proposals that would impose excessive evidentiary or adjudicative burdens (e.g., mandatory labor-market analyses for each case).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS will consider evidence submitted but will avoid instituting processes that would be administratively onerous or inconsistent with statutory approach.
